place-value.title: Place value: where a digit sits is what it is worth
place-value.recall: Cover the picture. What is the 7 worth in 2,740? And what does borrowing swap?

frames.caption: 345 is 3 hundreds, 4 tens and 5 ones — say what each digit is WORTH, not just what it is.
Each column is worth ten times the one on its right.
Ten of one column make one of the next — that is all borrowing and carrying are.

integers.title: Negative numbers on the number line
integers.recall: Cover it. Which way do you move for + (−3)? What is 2 − (−5)?

frames.caption: Start at −2. Adding 5 moves you five steps to the right: you land on 3.
Adding a negative number is the same as subtracting: you move left.
Taking away a negative turns you round: −(−4) is +4.

equal-groups.title: Multiplication is equal groups; division undoes it
equal-groups.recall: Cover it. Draw 2 × 6 as an array in your head. What is 20 ÷ 6, with its remainder?

frames.caption: 3 × 4 means three equal groups of four.
Lay the groups out as an array and turn it: the order of a multiplication does not change the answer.
Division asks how many equal groups fit; what cannot make a whole group is the remainder.

fractions.title: Equivalent fractions: cut finer, the amount stays
fractions.recall: Cover it. Give two fractions equal to 3/4. Why is 2/6 the same as 1/3?

frames.caption: A fraction is a number of equal parts: 1/2 is one of two.
Cut each half in two: twice as many parts, twice as many shaded — the same amount.
Multiply (or divide) the top and the bottom by the same number and the fraction is unchanged.

fdp.title: Fractions, decimals and percentages are one number
fdp.recall: Cover it. Write 3/4 as a decimal and a percent. What is 0.1 as a fraction?

frames.caption: Percent means 'out of a hundred'. 25 of these 100 squares are shaded.
The same shaded amount is 1/4, 0.25 and 25%.
Divide to get the decimal; multiply by 100 to get the percent.

bodmas.title: Order of operations
bodmas.recall: Cover it. Say BODMAS from memory. What is 10 − 6 ÷ 2?

frames.caption: Everyone must get the same answer, so there is an agreed order.
Brackets, Orders (powers), then Division and Multiplication, then Addition and Subtraction.
Multiply before you add — unless brackets say otherwise.

balance.title: An equation is a balance
balance.recall: Cover it. Solve 2x + 1 = 9 by doing the same to both sides. What did you do first, and why?

frames.caption: x + 3 = 7: the two sides balance.
Whatever you do to one side, do to the other, and it stays balanced.
Undo the + 3, and x is on its own: x = 4. Put it back in to check.

like-terms.title: Like terms: only the same kind can be added
like-terms.recall: Cover it. Simplify 5x + 2y − x + y. Why can't 3x and 3x² be added?

frames.caption: Terms are 'like' when the letters match exactly.
Gather each kind together.
Add the numbers in front (coefficients) of each kind. Unlike terms stay apart.

expand.title: Expanding brackets is finding an area

frames.caption: 3(x + 2) is the area of a rectangle 3 tall and x + 2 wide.
Find each part: 3 × x and 3 × 2. Add them: 3x + 6.
Factorising is the same picture backwards: find what both parts share.

indices.title: Laws of indices: count the factors
indices.recall: Cover it. Simplify x⁴ × x³ and y⁶ ÷ y². What is 5⁰, and why?

frames.caption: Write the factors out and count them: 2 + 3 = 5.
Dividing cancels factors: 5 − 2 = 3.
Follow the pattern down: each power is half the last, so anything to the power 0 is 1.

angles.title: Angles on a line, and in a triangle
angles.recall: Cover it. Two angles of a triangle are 70° and 45°. What is the third, and why?

frames.caption: A straight line is a half turn: the angles on it add to 180°.
Take any triangle with angles a, b and c.
Tear off the three corners and put them side by side: they make a straight line, 180°.

pythagoras.title: Pythagoras: the squares on the sides
pythagoras.recall: Cover it. A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. How long is the hypotenuse? Which side is c?

frames.caption: A right-angled triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5.
Build a square on each side: 9 small squares and 16 small squares exactly fill the 25.
Only for right-angled triangles. c is always the longest side.

circle.title: Circles: once round is π diameters
circle.recall: Cover it. A wheel has radius 7 cm. How far does it go in one turn (use π ≈ 22/7)?

frames.caption: The radius goes from the centre to the edge; the diameter goes right across.
Roll the circle out flat: its edge is just over three diameters long. That number is π.
Circumference is π × diameter. Area is π × radius squared.

gradient.title: Gradient: rise over run
gradient.recall: Cover it. What is the gradient of y = −3x + 4, and where does it cross the y-axis?

frames.caption: Pick two points on the line. How far across (run)? How far up (rise)?
Gradient is how much it goes up for each one across.
In y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c is where the line crosses the y-axis.

sohcahtoa.title: Trigonometry: name the sides from the angle
sohcahtoa.hook: SOH CAH TOA — Sine = Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite/Adjacent
sohcahtoa.recall: Cover it. Say SOH CAH TOA and what each part means. Which ratio links Opposite and Adjacent?

frames.caption: Stand at the angle θ: the side across from you is Opposite, the one beside you is Adjacent, the longest is the Hypotenuse.
Sine is Opposite over Hypotenuse, Cosine is Adjacent over Hypotenuse, Tangent is Opposite over Adjacent.
Label the sides, choose the ratio from the two you have, then calculate.

mean.title: The mean is levelling out
mean.recall: Cover it. Find the mean of 3, 7, 8 and 10. How is it different from the median?

frames.caption: Five stacks of different heights.
Move cubes from the tall stacks to the short ones until they are all the same height.
That level height is the mean: share the total out equally.

probability.title: Probability: count the equally likely outcomes
probability.recall: Cover it. A bag has 3 red and 5 blue. What is P(red)? P(not red)?

frames.caption: List every outcome. Two dice give 36 equally likely totals in this grid.
Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ all equally likely outcomes.
Every probability lies from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain); the chance something does NOT happen is 1 minus the chance it does.

ratio.title: Sharing in a ratio
ratio.recall: Cover it. Share ₦36 in the ratio 1 : 3. What is one part worth?

frames.caption: A ratio 2 : 3 means 5 equal parts: 2 for one, 3 for the other.
Add the parts, then find what one part is worth.
Multiply each person's parts by one part's value — then check they add up.

interest.title: Simple and compound interest
interest.recall: Cover it. ₦1,000 at 10% for 2 years: what is the simple interest? The compound amount?

frames.caption: Simple interest adds the same amount every year: 10% of what you first put in.
Compound interest pays interest on the interest, so it grows faster each year.
Simple interest is a straight line; compound interest curves upward.

logs.title: A logarithm asks: what power?
logs.recall: Cover it. What is log₂ 32? Write log₁₀ 1000 = 3 as a power.

frames.caption: Raising 2 to a power: 2³ = 8.
A logarithm asks the question backwards: what power of 2 gives 8? Answer: 3.
Every log is a power fact turned round: if bⁿ = x then log_b x = n.

word-classes.title: What job does each word do?
word-classes.recall: Cover it. In 'The old dog barked loudly', name the class of each word.

frames.caption: Look at what each word DOES in the sentence.
A noun names. A verb is the action (or a state, like 'is').
An adjective describes a noun; an adverb describes a verb. Decide by the job, not the word.

plurals.title: Making plurals
plurals.recall: Cover it. Give the plurals of fox, lady, key, woman and information.

frames.caption: Most nouns just add -s.
Add -es after s, x, ch, sh (you hear an extra syllable). A consonant + y becomes -ies.
Irregular plurals do not follow the rules — learn them as pairs.

agreement.title: Subject–verb agreement
agreement.recall: Cover it. Choose: 'The list of names (is/are) long.' 'Everybody (know/knows) the answer.'

frames.caption: One subject takes the -s verb; more than one does not.
Cross out the phrase in the middle: the verb agrees with the real subject, 'the box'.
'Each', 'everyone' and 'nobody' are singular. With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

apostrophe.title: The apostrophe: missing letters or belonging
apostrophe.recall: Cover it. Correct: 'The dog wagged it's tail.' 'The two boys bags.'

frames.caption: In a contraction, the apostrophe marks the missing letters.
Write the owner first, then add the apostrophe: one girl's, two girls', the children's.
Test it: if 'it is' fits, write it's. Otherwise it's its — like his and hers, no apostrophe.

homophones.title: There, their, they're — and other sound-alikes
homophones.recall: Cover it. Fill: '___ going to bring ___ books over ___.'

frames.caption: They sound the same; the meaning decides the spelling.
Find the clue inside each word: tHERE, the owner 'I' in thEIR, and the apostrophe in they're.
For any contraction, say the long form; if it fits, use the apostrophe.

tenses.title: Tenses on a timeline
tenses.recall: Cover it. Which tense is 'She has finished'? Draw 'They were playing' on a timeline.

frames.caption: Simple past, present and future: one dot each, at a point in time.
The continuous (be + -ing) is a stretch of time, still going on.
The perfect (have + past participle) is a past action joined to now: 'I have eaten' — so I am not hungry.

passive.title: Active and passive voice
passive.recall: Cover it. Make passive: 'The teacher marked the books.' Make active: 'The match was won by our team.'

frames.caption: Active: the doer (the dog) does the action.
Passive: the receiver comes first, the verb becomes 'was chased', and the doer moves to 'by …' — or disappears.
Use the passive when the doer is unknown or unimportant; otherwise the active is clearer.

reported.title: Reported speech: one step back in time
reported.recall: Cover it. Report: Tobi said, “I will come tomorrow.”

frames.caption: Direct speech gives the exact words.
Reporting moves each tense one step back into the past — and 'today' becomes 'that day'.
Change the person, step the tense back, and drop the quotation marks.

conditionals.title: Conditionals: how likely is the 'if'?
conditionals.recall: Cover it. Finish: 'If I were the principal, I ___.' Which conditional is it?

frames.caption: Zero for facts that are always true; first for a real, likely future.
Second for the imagined; third for a past that cannot be changed.
The further from reality, the further back the tense steps.

articles.title: A or an? Listen, don't look
articles.recall: Cover it. Choose a or an: ___ umbrella, ___ uniform, ___ hour, ___ MP3.

frames.caption: Choose by the first SOUND, not the first letter.
'Hour' starts with a vowel sound; 'university' starts with a 'y' sound.
'A/an' introduces something; 'the' points to one we already know.

stress.title: Word stress can change the word
stress.recall: Cover it. Mark the stress: 'Please conDUCT / CONduct the tests.' Which is the verb?

frames.caption: In every word of two or more syllables, one is stressed: louder, longer, higher.
Many two-syllable pairs stress the first syllable as a noun and the second as a verb.
Stressing a different word in a sentence changes what you mean.

roots.title: Word parts: roots, prefixes and suffixes
roots.hook: Keyword method: link each root to a word you already know — 'tele' as in television
roots.recall: Cover it. What do 'geo', 'graph' and 'auto' mean? Use them to explain 'autograph'.

frames.caption: Many English words are built from Greek and Latin parts. Biology = the study of life.
Learn one root and you can work out a family of words.
A prefix at the front, or a suffix at the end, changes the meaning in a predictable way.

figurative.title: Simile, metaphor, personification
figurative.recall: Cover it. Name each: 'as brave as a lion', 'the classroom was a zoo', 'the car coughed'.

frames.caption: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as'.
A metaphor says one thing IS another — no 'like' or 'as'.
Personification gives a thing human actions. In an exam, say what effect the comparison has.

peel.title: A strong paragraph: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link
peel.recall: Cover it. Say PEEL from memory, then write a P sentence for 'Phones should be allowed in school'.

frames.caption: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link — one paragraph, one idea.
Each sentence does one job.
Linking words show how one idea leads to the next.

who-whom.title: Who or whom? Swap in he or him
who-whom.hook: whoM = hiM — both end in m
who-whom.recall: Cover it. Choose: 'The man (who/whom) I met was kind.' 'The boy (whose/who's) phone rang left.'

frames.caption: Who does the action (like he); whom receives it (like him). Whom and him both end in m.
Answer the question in your head with he or him, then choose who or whom to match.
Whose shows belonging; which is for things; who's means 'who is'.

punctuation.title: Full stops, commas, semicolons and colons
punctuation.recall: Cover it. Punctuate: 'I was tired I had walked all day' — in two different correct ways.

frames.caption: A full stop ends a sentence; commas separate the items in a list.
A semicolon joins two complete sentences that are closely linked.
A colon says 'here it is': a list, an example or an explanation follows.

counting.title: Counting: one number for each thing
counting.recall: Cover it. Count back 5 from 32 — where do you land? Why does the last number you say tell you how many?

frames.caption: Touch each star once and say one number for it.
The last number you say is how many there are, whatever order you count in.
Counting back 4 is taking away 4: from 17 you land on 13.

adding.title: Adding: put the groups together
adding.recall: Cover it. Why is 25 + 38 the same as 38 + 25? Work out 476 + 258 and say each carry.

frames.caption: Adding puts two groups together and counts the whole: 3 + 4 = 7.
The order you add in does not change the total.
Add each column from the ones; ten in a column carries 1 to the next column.

zero.title: Zero: the number that changes nothing when you add it
zero.recall: Cover it. Which of these equal 47: 47 + 0, 47 × 0, 47 − 0, 0 + 47? Why?

frames.caption: Zero is how many are in an empty basket, so 5 + 0 = 5.
Take every mango away and none are left: a number minus itself is 0.
Adding or taking away 0 leaves a number as it is; a number minus itself, or times 0, is 0.

subtracting.title: Subtraction: how many are left, and how far apart
subtracting.recall: Cover it. Kemi has ₦750 and Sola has ₦480. How much more has Kemi? Check by counting up.

frames.caption: Subtraction as taking away: 8 − 3 leaves 5.
“How much more” is the gap between the two amounts: also a subtraction.
Count up from the smaller amount to the bigger: what you add is the difference.

comparing.title: Comparing numbers: more, less or equal
comparing.recall: Cover it. Which sign goes in 63 ☐ 36? Put 3,091, 3,190 and 3,109 in order, smallest first.

frames.caption: Pair the things off one to one: whichever row has some left over has more.

frames.alt: The sign points to the smaller
frames.caption: Compare the tens first; the open side of < or > faces the bigger number.
Line the numbers up by place value; the first column that differs decides. More digits always means bigger.

factors.title: Factors come in pairs; multiples go on for ever
factors.recall: Cover it. List the factors of 18 in pairs. Is 4,512 divisible by 3? By 9?

frames.caption: Every way to make 12 into a rectangle gives a pair of factors.
The multiples of 3 are its times table, and they never stop.
A number divides by 3 (or 9) exactly when the sum of its digits does.

hcf-lcm.title: Primes, HCF and LCM: share out the prime factors
hcf-lcm.recall: Cover it. Find the HCF and LCM of 8 and 12 from their prime factors.

frames.caption: A prime number can only be laid out as one row: its only factors are 1 and itself.
Split each number until every branch ends in a prime.
The HCF multiplies the primes both share; the LCM multiplies every prime either needs.

unit-conversion.title: Converting units: same amount, different-sized pieces
unit-conversion.recall: Cover it. Change 3.2 km to metres and 1,500 g to kilograms. How many minutes are in 1 h 45 min?

frames.alt: One kilometre is a thousand metres
frames.caption: 1 km and 1,000 m are the same length, cut into pieces of a different size.
Going to a smaller unit, multiply; going to a bigger unit, divide.
Hours and minutes go in sixties, so 1.5 hours is 1 hour 30 minutes.

rounding.title: Rounding: the nearest value, and the range it hides
rounding.recall: Cover it. Round 5,649 to the nearest 100 and 0.03081 to 2 s.f. A bag is 40 kg to the nearest kg: what are its bounds?

frames.caption: Find the two hundreds it sits between; it rounds to the nearer one. Halfway or more rounds up.
Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit; the zeros in front only hold places.
A rounded measurement could be up to half a unit either side: those ends are its bounds.

speed-dst.title: Speed: the distance gone in each hour
speed-dst.recall: Cover it. A bus goes 90 km in 1 h 30 min. What is its speed? Why is average speed not the average of the speeds?

frames.caption: A danfo at 60 km/h covers another 60 km in every hour.
Speed is distance divided by time — with the time in the unit the speed uses.
Average speed is total distance ÷ total time — not the average of the speeds.

bar-model.title: Word problems: draw it, then write it
bar-model.recall: Cover it. Two numbers add to 50 and one is 8 more than the other. Draw the bars, then write the equation.

frames.caption: Draw a bar for each amount: Ade's is Bola's bar plus ₦500.
Take away the extra and what is left is equal bars: share it out.
The bars are the equation: name the unknown, write what the story says, solve, then check.

sequences.title: Sequences: a start plus equal steps
sequences.recall: Cover it. Find the 20th term of 4, 7, 10, … Is 5, 10, 20, 40 an AP or a GP? Say how you know.

frames.caption: An arithmetic sequence starts somewhere and adds the same step each time.
To reach the nth term you take one step fewer than n: a + (n − 1)d.
An arithmetic progression adds the same step; a geometric progression multiplies by the same ratio.

inequalities.title: Inequalities: a whole range of answers
inequalities.recall: Cover it. Solve 3 − 2x ≥ 9 and draw it on a number line. Is the circle open or filled?

frames.caption: An inequality is a range: open circle when the end is not included, filled when it is.
Do the same to both sides, just as you would to an equation.
Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.

simultaneous.title: Simultaneous equations: the one pair that fits both
simultaneous.recall: Cover it. Solve x + y = 10 and x − y = 4 by elimination, then check it by substitution.

frames.caption: Each equation is a line of points; the solution is the one point on both lines.
Substitution: when one equation says what a letter is, put that into the other.
Elimination: add or subtract the equations so one letter cancels — the same answer, (3, 4).

algebraic-fractions.title: Adding fractions needs same-sized parts — letters too
algebraic-fractions.recall: Cover it. Write x/4 + x/6 as a single fraction. Why is 1/2 + 1/3 not 2/5?

frames.caption: A half and a third are pieces of different sizes, so they cannot be added yet.
Cut both into sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
With letters it is the same: a common denominator first, then add the numerators.

surds.title: Surds: take out the square, add only like surds

frames.caption: Split the number into a square times what is left: the square comes out as its root.
Like surds add like like terms; different surds stay apart.
To clear a root from the bottom, multiply by a fraction that equals 1.

en-synonyms.title: Synonyms and antonyms: same side or opposite ends
en-synonyms.recall: Cover it. Give a synonym and an antonym for 'brave'. What is the opposite of 'regular'?

frames.caption: Synonyms sit together on the same side; antonyms sit at opposite ends.

frames.alt: Nearest in meaning, in this sentence
frames.caption: 'Nearest in meaning' means nearest in THIS sentence: swap each option in and read it aloud.
An antonym must be the same kind of word: an adjective for an adjective.

en-prepositions.title: Prepositions: where and when
en-prepositions.recall: Cover it. Fill: 'I was born ___ 2012, ___ a Sunday, ___ dawn.' Correct: 'Let us discuss about it.'

frames.caption: A preposition shows where one thing is in relation to another.
IN for the biggest stretch of time, ON for a day, AT for a point.
Some words choose their own preposition and some need none: learn them in pairs.

en-question-tags.title: Question tags: flip the sentence
en-question-tags.recall: Cover it. Add the tags: 'Chidi was late, ___?' 'They won't come, ___?' 'Bisi sings well, ___?'

frames.caption: A positive sentence takes a negative tag.
A negative sentence takes a positive tag.
Repeat the helping verb (do, have, can, are) and the pronoun — never a one-size 'isn't it?'.

en-vowels.title: Vowel sounds: short, long and gliding
en-vowels.recall: Cover it. Is the vowel in 'pool' short or long? Which has a diphthong: 'bed', 'bead' or 'bide'?

frames.caption: A long vowel is held longer — and it changes the word: ship, sheep.
Say each pair aloud: the only thing that changes is the vowel.
A diphthong is two vowels in one syllable: the mouth glides from the first to the second.

en-th-sh.title: th, sh, ch, j and zh: where the tongue goes
en-th-sh.recall: Cover it. Which sound is in 'thin' and which in 'then'? Sort: shoe, pleasure, cheap, judge.

frames.caption: For th, put the tip of your tongue between your teeth and blow — add your voice for 'this'.
sh and zh are a pair, ch and j are a pair: the same tongue, but the right-hand one adds your voice.
English letters often hide the sound: -tion says sh, -sure says zh.

en-silent-clusters.title: Count the sounds, not the letters
en-silent-clusters.recall: Cover it. Which letter is silent in 'thumb', 'knot' and 'castle'? How many sounds are in 'ship' and in 'splash'?

frames.caption: Silent letters are written but not said: lamb, listen, knee, write, hour.
A cluster is two or three consonants with no vowel between: say them together, adding nothing.
Letters and sounds do not match one to one: count what you hear.

en-rhymes.title: Rhymes are matched by sound, not spelling
en-rhymes.recall: Cover it. Which pair rhymes: 'hair/there', 'bear/fear', 'blood/mood'? Say them aloud first.

frames.caption: Words rhyme when the last vowel sound and everything after it match.
The spelling can differ: bite, light and height all rhyme, because they sound alike.
And the same spelling can hide different sounds: cow and low do not rhyme. Say them aloud.

en-intonation.title: Intonation: the tune of a sentence
en-intonation.recall: Cover it. Rising or falling: 'Is it raining?' 'What is your name?' 'I live in Enugu.'

frames.caption: The voice falls at the end of a statement: it tells.
The voice rises at the end of a yes/no question: it asks.
A wh- question (who, where, why) falls like a statement; let a statement rise and it becomes a question.

en-phrasal-idioms.title: Phrasal verbs and idioms: more than their parts
en-phrasal-idioms.recall: Cover it. What does 'look after' mean? And 'to bury the hatchet'?

frames.caption: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word, and together they mean something new.
Change the small word and the meaning changes: give up, give in, give out, give away.
An idiom cannot be worked out word by word: learn it as one unit, with its meaning.

en-modals.title: Modal verbs: how sure, how necessary
en-modals.recall: Cover it. Correct: 'He should goes home.' Which is surer: 'It may be Ada' or 'It must be Ada'?

frames.caption: Modals show how sure the speaker is: 'might' is a maybe, 'must' and 'will' are near certain.
They also show ability (can), permission (may), duty (must) and advice (should).
After a modal comes the bare verb. 'Must have done' is a confident guess about the past.

en-gerunds.title: -ing or to? The verb in front decides
en-gerunds.recall: Cover it. Choose: 'I enjoy (to read / reading).' 'She refused (paying / to pay).' What is 'remember to lock' versus 'remember locking'?

frames.caption: Some verbs take -ing (I enjoy swimming); others take to (I want to swim).
A gerund is an -ing word used as a noun. After a preposition, use -ing: 'interested in reading'.
With stop, remember and forget, choosing -ing or to changes the meaning.

en-main-idea.title: The main idea holds up the details
en-main-idea.recall: Cover it. What three things does a summary leave out? Summarise a paragraph you read today in two sentences.

frames.caption: The main idea is the one point every other sentence supports — a table top on its legs.

frames.alt: Keep the points, drop the rest
frames.caption: To summarise, keep the points and drop the examples, the repeats and the decoration.
Write each point as one short sentence of your own — numbered, if the question asks for points.

en-inference.title: Reading between the lines
en-inference.recall: Cover it. 'Ngozi stared at her plate and said nothing.' What can you infer, and which clue told you?

frames.caption: The text does not say it is raining: you infer it from a clue plus what you already know.
When a word is new, the words around it are the clue: 'we could hardly move' means teeming is very crowded.
When asked for your own words, change the key word — copying it from the text earns nothing.

en-fact-opinion.title: Fact or opinion? Can it be checked?
en-fact-opinion.recall: Cover it. Fact or opinion: 'Rice is grown in Kebbi.' 'Jollof rice is the tastiest food.' Which word told you?

frames.caption: A fact can be checked and proved; an opinion is someone's judgement.
Words that judge — best, beautiful, should, I think — signal an opinion.
One sentence can mix the two: split it and test each part.

en-register.title: Register: dress your words for the occasion
en-register.recall: Cover it. Make formal: 'The kids were gonna wreck the place.' Who is the audience of a PTA speech?

frames.caption: Register is how formal your language is — chosen by who you are speaking or writing to.
Formal writing avoids slang and contractions: 'gonna' becomes 'going to', 'kids' becomes 'children'.
Before writing a speech, report or article, ask who will read it and why: that decides the register.

en-letters.title: Three letters, three layouts
en-letters.recall: Cover it. Draw the formal layout from memory. How do you end a letter that begins 'Dear Mrs Adeyemi'?

frames.caption: A formal letter has two addresses, a title, 'Dear Sir/Madam' and 'Yours faithfully'.
An informal letter, to a friend or relative, has one address, no title, and ends with your first name.
Match the ending to the greeting: 'Sir' → faithfully; a name → sincerely; a friend → your first name.

en-concise.title: Join and trim: say it in fewer words
en-concise.recall: Cover it. Join: 'It rained. The match went on.' Shorten: 'He is a man who is very kind.'

frames.caption: Join two short sentences with a word that shows how they relate: although, because, when.
A 'who' or 'which' clause folds one sentence inside another.
Cut the words that add nothing: 'due to the fact that' is just 'because'.

en-usage.title: Common errors: say it the standard way
en-usage.recall: Cover it. Correct: 'Borrow me your book.' 'She gave me many advices.' 'Myself and Ada will go.'

frames.caption: Each of these is common in speech but marked wrong in the exam.
Some nouns are uncountable: no -s and no 'a'. Count them with 'a piece of'.
Watch the doubled words — 'more better', 'the both' — and 'myself' where 'I' belongs.

en-collocations.title: Collocations: words that go together
en-collocations.recall: Cover it. Make or do: ___ an effort, ___ the dishes, ___ friends. Which is right: 'strong rain' or 'heavy rain'?

frames.caption: Some words simply go together: we MAKE a mistake but DO our homework.
Adjectives choose their nouns too: heavy rain, strong tea, a high fever.
Note new words in chunks, the way they are used: pay attention, catch a cold, keep a secret.

en-field-health-law.title: Words of health, law and government
en-field-health-law.hook: Word parts: cardi = heart, -itis = swelling, -ologist = expert
en-field-health-law.recall: Cover it. What does a dermatologist treat? Who brings a case to court? Which arm of government makes laws?

frames.caption: Medical words are built from parts: cardi (heart) + -ologist (expert) = a heart doctor.
In court the plaintiff brings the case, the defendant answers it, and the judge gives the verdict.
Government has three arms: the legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out, the judiciary interprets them.

en-field-trade-media.title: Words of farming, trade, money and the media
en-field-trade-media.recall: Cover it. Who buys in bulk, the wholesaler or the retailer? Income ₦20,000, costs ₦26,000 — profit or loss? What does an editor do?

frames.caption: Trade words follow the goods: the farmer harvests, the wholesaler buys in bulk, the retailer sells to the consumer.
Profit is what is left of the income after the costs; if the costs are bigger, it is a loss.
Media words follow the news from reporter to editor to broadcast; upload sends data, download receives it.

en-essays.title: Narrative and descriptive essays
en-essays.recall: Cover it. Draw the story mountain and label it. Write one sentence about your street for each of the five senses.

frames.caption: A narrative tells a story: an opening, a problem that builds to a climax, then a resolution and an ending.
A descriptive essay paints a picture: use all five senses, not just sight.
A narrative moves through time; a description stays in one place and looks closely.
